chunks: From him, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from Safwan ibn Yahya, from Sa'id ibn Yasir, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him) who said:

I asked him about a man who gave money to another man, saying, 'I am giving you the money so that the profit belongs to my daughter, so-and-so.' Then the man decided, after giving the money, to take twenty-five dinars from it and buy a slave-girl for his grandson. Afterwards, the man died, and a dispute arose between the two slave-girls and the boy (or one of them said to him): 'You are marrying your slave-girl unlawfully. Our father bought her for you from our money, which he gave to so-and-so, and he bought a slave-girl for him from it. So you are marrying her unlawfully; she is not permissible for you.' The young man refrained from the slave-girl. I asked, 'What do you think about that?' He said, 'Is not the man who gave the money the father of the two slave-girls, and he is the grandfather of the boy, and he is the one who bought the slave-girl?' I said, 'Yes.' He said, 'Then let him approach his slave-girl, since he is the one who gave and he is the one who took.'
ai.seo_question: What is the Islamic legal ruling on marriage to a slave-girl purchased with partnership profits for a specific beneficiary?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (AS) clarifies that the permissibility of marriage between the grandson and the slave-girl hinges on the principle of effective ownership (milkiyah) rather than the source of funds alone; since the grandfather provided the capital and purchased the slave-girl, she is considered his property, making the marriage valid. This ruling underscores the Shia jurisprudential emphasis on the intent (niyyah) and actual acquisition in financial partnerships, distinguishing between the provider of capital and the ultimate owner of the acquired asset. It serves as a key precedent for resolving disputes in mudarabah where assets are acquired for specific beneficiaries.
